sentences.text: Protoavis is typically portrayed as a two-legged archosaur resembling poposaurids and rauisuchids from the same era.
Its skull features an extremely narrow parietal bone and very broad, T-shaped frontals that create lateral wings where postorbitals are missing.
Chatterjee argued that the spine showed bird-like traits such as heterocoelous centra, hypapophyses, and reduced neural spines.
However, the well-preserved wrist and hand bones of Protoavis display features that are distinctly non-avian.
Fossils were found in 1984 at a quarry in the Texas panhandle within the Dockum Group.
The holotype and paratype specimens were located in different places and were disarticulated and unassociated.
Reconstructions depict Protoavis as a meat-eating bird with front-facing eyes, suggesting a nocturnal or crepuscular lifestyle.
The main predators in its environment were poposaurids like Postosuchus.
The fossils represent a jumbled collection of disarticulated bones resulting from a mass mortality event caused by a flash flood.
Protoavis is classified within the parent group Theropoda and in the class Reptilia.
The paleoclimate of the Dockum Group was subtropical with a distinct dry and wet season pattern marked by monsoonal rains.

The true classification of Protoavis is controversial with many different interpretations of what the animal actually is. Many paleontologists doubt that Protoavis is a bird or that all remains come from a single species due to unconvincing avian features in the fragmentary material. Data suggest that prokinesis in the skull of Protoavis is questionable and that the specimen likely displays a conventional opisthostylic quadrate. The presence of poorly developed hypapophyses on non-avian vertebrae is regarded as mild convergence rather than evidence of avian affinity. Researchers question whether the pectoral girdle features described by Chatterjee were actually present in Protoavis because the fossil preservation is poor.
